name: cmix
listed_description: A lossless data compression program that aims for the highest compression ratios at the cost of speed.
reason: No speed claim and no numbers at all: the README (version 21, 2024-09-10) and the repo page state that cmix optimises compression ratio at the cost of high CPU and memory use (32 GB RAM recommended) and contain no benchmark table or comparison against paq8, xz, zstd or any other compressor; the only advice is to build with -Ofast -march=native. The project's own page (byronknoll.com/cmix.html) and the Large Text Compression Benchmark (mattmahoney.net) are blocked here, and any comparison there would be on compressed size, not faster-than. It is a ratio-leader, not a faster-than-baseline entry.

name: heatshrink
listed_description: Data compression/decompression library for embedded and ... (lead text truncated; repo description: data compression/decompression library optimized for embedded and real-time systems)
reason: Claims are about memory and bounded CPU per call (as low as 50 bytes, under 300 bytes for many cases), not speed against a named baseline. The README gives no numbers against zlib, LZO or lzjb; the repo's benchmark/ directory holds one shell script that sweeps heatshrink's own window and lookahead settings over the Canterbury corpus and reports its own ratios. The author's blog post (spin.atomicobject.com) is blocked and its search snippet describes only a ratio table across heatshrink settings. The one independent comparison found (BrianPugh/tamp README, enwik8 on an M3 MacBook Air) shows heatshrink slower than zlib at decompression (0.67 s vs 0.578 s), slower at compression without its index (27.40 s vs 3.65 s) and 4.42 s with the index, and bigger output than zlib on most Silesia files; its memory table gives heatshrink 1 << (windowBits + 1) bytes against zlib's (1 << (windowBits + 2)) + 7KB, a formula not a measurement, and memory is not a speed metric.
